extracted.intended_audience: classicists, philologists, editors/translators of ancient poetry and students of classical poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and formal definitions from a classical-poetics commentary covering phonology (syllable/sound), categories of words/names, and practical/esthetic rules for composing or judging epic and tragic poetry (unity, metre, diction, variation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllable definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllaba quidem est sonus compositus SIGNIFICANS, compositus ex elemento vocali et non-vocali; G and R without A are not syllaba, since syllables form only with A; GRA is a syllable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect variation of these elements in different meters; syllablehood depends on presence of the vowel element and interacts with metric forms, length, correction, and accent (acu/min e) — consult metric variation when scanning lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunction and separative sounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Coniunctio is a sonus compositus non significans (e.g., 'quidem', 'et nonne'); separativa is a sonus compositus non significans indicating beginning, end or termination (e.g., 'et', 'atque', 'propter', 'autem').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between signifying and non-signifying composite sounds when analyzing prosody and syntax; recognise conjunctions and separatives as non-significant sonorities that nevertheless affect metrical composition and placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence (sententia) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Sententia est sonus significans compositus cuius singulae partes significant separatim; not every sentence is composed of a verb (a sentence can be without verbs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating syntactic form, note that a sentence's parts can each carry separate meaning (nomina, verba); definitions may function as sentences without full verbal morphology (e.g., 'Cleonos ambulat').

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of speech distinctions (nomen/verbum/casus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nomen is a composite sound indicating without reference to time; verbum is a signifying sound which indicates time (present, past, future); casus of noun or verb indicates grammatical relations in sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these grammatical distinctions to judge correctness of form and the temporal/significative function of words in metrical or rhetorical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of names (omne nomen est ...)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omne nomen est aut proprium aut glossa aut translatum aut ornamentum aut factum aut actum aut separatum aut mutatum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and label names in these categories when assessing diction: a 'proprium' (proper name) used by one people, 'glossa' (foreign sense), 'transferentia' (translation/transfer), 'nomen factum' (poetic coinage), etc.; examples and local usages matter for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of transferentia (translation of names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transferentia nominis est translatio nominis alieni sive a genere ad genus aliquod magis, sive a specie magis (translation by genus/species or by analogy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations or transferred names may be valid stylistically (e.g., using a species to stand for a genus) but must respect analogy and customary usage; examples show possible acceptable and unacceptable transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomen factum (poetic coinage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nomen factum est nomen quod ponit poeta, when a poet coins a name that does not denote the universal class of people (examples: terms for growing horns, sacerdotal epithets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic coinages are legitimate but should be judged on their clarity and conventionality — they may become accepted or be ridiculed depending on usage and intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producted/separated/varied names (nomen productum/separatum/variatum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nomen productum et separatum is produced from vocal elements (long or with adventitious syllable); variatum occurs where part of the name is removed and the form is altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing morphological variation in names, account for whether the poet uses long letters, short substitutions, or omits parts; such manipulations affect meter and recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphological rules for name endings (gender/number)
rubrics_metrics.description: Masculine names end in NUM, RO and SIGMA (with Ionic forms CsI and Psi as composites); feminine names end in vocal letters long (ETA, final 0) such as ALPHA and IOTA; names in the middle end in NU or SIGMA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these morphological patterns when evaluating form and agreement in verse; they explain typical inflectional behavior relevant to scanning and to perceived 'rightness' of forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue of eloquence: celebre and mancum
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtus vero eloquii est ut sit celebre, mancum; 'celebre' arises from use of proper names and remembrance; 'casta et variata' is achieved by using alien and splendid names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good diction favors celebrated (well-known) and concise (mancum) expression; tasteful variety and use of apt names enhance eloquence. Excessive mixing or awkward substitutions can harm style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing glosses/translations improperly (barbarismus, aenigmata)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one mixes translations, glosses, productions improperly, the result is barbarismus or aenigmata; such mixing is ridiculed (poet mocked) and is generally inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of combining proprietary names, translations and glosses in ways that upset convention or intelligibility. Some mixing (when customary) is acceptable; arbitrary or incongruous mixings are faulted and produce ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper substitution of proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: If proper names are changed where customary in the language, the substitution may be good; but unnatural substitutions cause incongruity (ridiculum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate substitutions according to custom and appropriateness to the language/metric context — acceptable substitutions follow use; unacceptable ones produce ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of names in metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Conveniens omnibus iis quae differunt, hoc cernitur ... ubi ponuntur nomina in metro; if proper names are altered, meter must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When altering or substituting names, ensure they fit metrically; meter-sensitive placement of names is crucial to maintain poetic decorum and avoid indecorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the poem (initium, medium, finis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carmen ... quod habet initium et medium et finem; a perfect opus should have a beginning, middle and end and be treated as a single whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose or judge works for narrative unity: cohesive structure, coherent progression, and an appropriate terminal point. Fragmentary collections or loose series of episodes may lack the necessary unity unless intentionally episodic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performers and songs should cohere around one finished work
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantatores et carmina circa opus unum perfectum totum — singers and songs should be disposed around one complete work (having a proper beginning, middle, end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In performance and editorial practice, aim for or preserve coherent cycles rather than scattering songs/episodes disconnectedly across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient terminus (adequate length and control of beginning/end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminus sufficiens longitudinis is that limit in which power over beginning and end exists; this limit determines adequacy of length for composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a composition attains sufficient length to enact its intended beginning, middle and end; genre expectations (e.g., tragedy with single session) influence what counts as sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrum must suit the poem (metric appropriateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrum carminum modo convenit ab experientia; altering narration while using a different metre may be indecorous; meter should be chosen consistent with poetic nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose meters based on experiential suitability to the genre: do not impose a meter alien to the poem's established practice (example: one should not construct a long system in a metre unlike that of the poem), and recognise that some meters admit glosses and translations more readily than others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meteral stability and allowance for glosses/translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrum firmius et numerosius is preferable across meters; meter receives glossas and translationes and admits increments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger rhythmic/meter choices withstand inserted glosses and translations better; when adding explanatory words or translated terms, account for metrical resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of diction (brevity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetae convenit ut quae loquatur sint pauca; imitators are often verbose; Homer is praised for brevity and knowing what to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise expression in poetry; excessive prolixity is judged inferior and may signal mere imitation rather than true poetic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety in introductions to avoid satiety
rubrics_metrics.description: Introductions should be dissimiles; similar introductions cause satiety and make tragedies fall (lose effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary opening passages and devices across works to sustain audience interest; avoid repetitious formulae that produce boredom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce the marvelous (mirabile) appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Oportet facere in tragoediis mirabile; in epic and epe it is fitting that marvellous events occur according to analogy (they should not display the agent), and such elements should move the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include wondrous elements to create admiration, but place them according to analogy and decorum within the scene; their treatment differs by genre and must not violate recognition or plausibility within the poetic frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of imitation (limit imitation to few things)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitator should imitate in few things; imitation in many parts is common among lesser poets but the true poet imitates sparingly and effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When emulating predecessors, select limited, essential features rather than wholesale copying; originality with selective imitation is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs. tragic compositional allowances
rubrics_metrics.description: Carmen amborum est compositum; Ilias simplex et passiva, Oda composita: arts of narration and metre differ in length and constitution; epe may be longer and permit large narration, tragedy is more constrained by scene and performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate structure with genre-specific expectations: epic (epe) naturally permits expansive narration and episodic material; tragedy is bound to stageable sessions and requires tighter handling of parts and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indecorous metric-narrative alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: It is turpe if one changes the narration and uses a metre unsuited (example: Chaeremon's failing); a system long in a metre different from the poem is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mismatch long theoretical metrical systems with the established metre of the poem; maintain customary metric practice to preserve decorum and appropriateness.
